summary: The IAB's recommended policy on distributing Internet identifier assignment, and on dropping the connected status requirement. It is informational and not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The people in charge say who should hand out network numbers, and that you no longer have to be plugged in to get one.

subtitle: The IAB's advice to spread out the handing-out of network numbers and to stop tying registration to "connected" status.

tldr.problem: One central registry assigned all network and autonomous system numbers, the Internet was growing and going international, and a "connected" status tied to US Government sponsorship no longer made sense.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB recommends that the Internet Registry delegate blocks of numbers to approved organizations, drop "connected" status, record each network's acceptable use and transit policy, and allow any registered network into the DNS.
tldr.outcome: This is an informational statement of the IAB's official view sent to the Federal Networking Council, not a standard.

today: RFC 1174 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the unit metadata. It records the IAB's recommendations to the FNC and does not itself specify a standard.

sections.title: Two Recommendations to the FNC
sections.content:
RFC 1174 carries two recommendations from the Internet Activities Board (IAB) to the Federal Networking Council (FNC). The memo is informational, states the official view of the IAB, and does not specify a standard.

The first suggests distributing the function of assigning network and autonomous system numbers. The second suggests dropping the notion of connected status in favor of recording the acceptable use policy and traffic access policy of each network. It also says that any registered network may be entered into the DNS database whatever its connected status.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two pieces of advice: let more people hand out network numbers, and stop making networks ask permission to be listed.

sections.title: Distributing Identifier Assignment
sections.content:
The Internet has always used a central Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) for numeric identifiers. The IANA function is performed by USC Information Sciences Institute. For network and autonomous system numbers, the IANA has placed the work with an Internet Registry (IR), performed by SRI International at its Network Information Center (DDN-NIC).

With rapid growth and internationalization, the memo says it is timely to delegate more. It also notes that network identifiers of class A and B type will become an increasingly scarce commodity that needs careful handling.

The proposed method keeps the central IANA and IR. The IR would stay the principal registry and keep the list of root Domain Name System servers and a database of registered nets and autonomous systems. In addition it would allocate blocks of numbers to organizations approved by the Coordinating Committee for Intercontinental Research Networking (CCIRN) and delegate further assignment authority to them. At first the IR would act as default registry where no delegated registry exists. Copies of the database would go to each delegated registry, but updates would remain centralized at the IR. Host domain name registration should continue as it is.
sections.plainLanguage: One office hands out all the street numbers. The advice is to let trusted offices in other places hand out blocks of numbers too, while one office keeps the master list.

sections.title: Why Connected Status Had to Go
sections.content:
The memo traces how numbers were first assigned only to organizations in the research effort, then to other organizations with US Government sponsorship. Commercial use of the Internet protocols led to private networks that wanted numbers without linking to the federally sponsored system. The IR began assigning numbers to everyone who asked, and marked networks permitted to link to the global Internet with connected status, which meant a US Government sponsor had sanctioned the link.

The memo argues this no longer fits. Intermediate-level networks serve a wide range of users, some with no restrictions at all, and non-US networks should not all be bound by US criteria; only the traffic they send through the federally sponsored networks must meet the federal criteria. In its words, there is no longer a simple binary correlation between connected status and acceptable use policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Long ago, only certain approved groups were let onto the network. Now many kinds of groups use it, so a simple yes-or-no pass no longer works.

sections.title: The Replacement: Recorded Policies
sections.content:
The memo recommends three actions for the Internet Registry:

  • Drop all reference to connected status in its databases and registration forms.
  • Ask each applicant for a network or autonomous system number for a brief statement of acceptable network usage, access and transit policy for external traffic, and gather such statements for networks already registered. They should be available online and widely publicized.
  • Allow any registered network to be entered into the Domain Name Server database, regardless of connected status.

Attributes that might be tracked include country codes and conformance to the acceptable use policy of networks such as NSFNET, MILNET, NSI, ESnet and NORDUnet. Under the proposal the IR registers and administers the number space but does not enforce policy, and the memo expects that this will make it easy later to spread the IR function over several centers, for example on different continents.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one pass that says connected or not, each network writes down what traffic it will carry, and everybody can look it up.

sections.title: Policy-Based Routing and DNS
sections.content:
Acting on use policies needs policy-based routing (PBR). The memo says the PBR available at the time works at the level of a whole network, which is more fine-grained than connected status but still coarse. A company could be unable to send legitimate research traffic if the same network also carries commercial traffic, and might have to define several networks to carry different policies. So government-sponsored networks will sometimes rely on self-policing by traffic sources. The memo mentions an IETF project to build a more general PBR that could give control to individual hosts and possibly users.

An attachment on the DNS says the DNS maps host names to IP addresses and delivers electronic mail. The past policy tied inclusion in the root servers' database to approval by a US Government agency. The IAB endorses a Federal Engineering Planning Group recommendation that naming and routing be completely decoupled, and that no US Government sponsor be required for domain name or address registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling the network which traffic to carry works for a whole building at once, not for each person. The advice also says that having your name in the phone book should not depend on your permission to connect.
